title: 9) Better Figures

## Assigned Readings

- Title: **Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures**
- Author(s): Rougier N., Droettboom M., Bourne P.
- Year: 2014
- Journal: PLOS Computational Biology
- <https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833>
- <doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003833>



## Reflections

::: {.callout-note title="bCourses Submission"}
Submit your answers---to the following questions---to the corresponding 
assignment in bCourses.

Accepted formats: PDF, HTML, MS Word (`.docx`), or Google Doc
:::


## Reflection 1: Breaking Free from the Plotting Library

- Open a script or file containing a chart you generated recently for a project or assignment.
- Did you critically think about the color palette, line weights, and spacing, 
or did you simply hit `plt.show()` or accept whatever visual theme the software generated by default?


## Reflection 2: Evaluating Your Caption Autonomy

- Imagine a peer reviewer crops a single chart out of your last lab report or essay, 
completely removing it from the surrounding paragraphs.
- If they stare *only* at that image and its attached caption box, can they fully 
understand your conclusion, or would they descend into confusion trying to guess 
what your visual markers mean?
- Why do we habitually write captions as short, lazy titles instead of rich explanations?


## Reflection 3: Stripping the "Chartjunk"

- Reflect on a time you were building a slide presentation or document and 
spent hours playing with color wheels, fonts, or drop-shadow effects.
- Was that aesthetic labor genuinely aimed at making your data patterns easier to read, 
or were you subconsciously using visual flashiness to distract from weak 
sample sizes or sloppy data variance?
- Where does helpful design end and "data cloaking" begin?


## Reflection 4: The Screen vs. The Sheet Reality Check

- Think about how your instructor or target audience will physically consume your next report.
- Do you actively test your color selections under grayscale or different viewing 
modes before exporting, or do you blindly assume that what looks pretty on your 
laptop screen will translate globally?


## Reflection 5: Deciding the Message Before the Code

- Think about your typical programming workflow.
- Do you blindly type plotting commands hoping a meaningful pattern accidentally emerges on the screen?
- How can sketching a mockup chart on scrap paper *before* writing code protect you from chasing random data noise?



## Rubric

::: {.callout-important}
Generic responses that do not mention a specific 
past assignment name or unique piece of code from your own experience will 
receive a score of zero.
:::

- **Full Credit (3 Points)**: Response is highly specific, names unique personal 
or localized constraints, and explicitly connects the personal experience 
back to the prompt in each question. Clearly written by a human.

- **Partial Credit (1-2 Points)**: Response is correct but uses vague or generic 
examples (e.g., "I lost a file once" instead of naming the script). Sounds like 
a generic summary an AI could have written.

- **No Credit (0 Points)**: Response relies entirely on abstract definitions, 
fails to provide personal context, or uses copy-pasted text from a webpage
or AI tool.
